title: extends / super
description: extends sets the prototype chain; super() calls the parent constructor; super.method() calls a parent method from an override.

notes: In a subclass constructor you MUST call super(...) before touching this — otherwise ReferenceError.
super.method() inside a method calls the parent version; super alone in a constructor calls the parent constructor.
instanceof walks the prototype chain — a Dog is also an Animal.

questions.q: Which keyword sets up class inheritance?
questions.explain: `extends` is what links `Dog.prototype` to `Animal.prototype`; `super` is what you call once that chain exists, not what creates it.

questions.q: What happens if you use `this` before calling super() in a subclass constructor?
questions.explain: In a derived constructor `this` stays uninitialized until `super()` returns — reading it early throws `ReferenceError: Must call super constructor...`. That is why `super(name)` precedes `this.breed = breed`.

questions.q: Inside an overridden method, how do you call the parent version?
questions.explain: `super.speak()` resolves on the parent prototype while keeping `this` as the instance. `Animal.prototype.speak.call(this)` does the same by hand — it works, but it hard-codes the parent name and breaks the moment the chain changes.

questions.q: For `class Dog extends Animal {}` and `const d = new Dog()`, what is `d instanceof Animal`?
questions.explain: `instanceof` walks the whole prototype chain, and `extends` put `Animal.prototype` on it — so `d` is an instance of both `Dog` and `Animal`.

exercises.prompt: Override speak() and call the parent version with super.
Add a subclass field and verify instanceof walks up the chain.

L3.prompt: Build `Animal` with describe() returning the name, and `Dog extends Animal` whose describe() returns parent describe + " the " + breed. Log `new Dog("Rex", "lab").describe()`.
hints: Call super(name) first in the Dog constructor.
In Dog.describe(), compose super.describe() with " the " + this.breed.
